planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring once soil has warmed, spacing plants generously to allow for a broad, rounded mature habit.

directions: Unlike most lavandins bred for deep violet spikes, 'Alba' produces clean white flowers on long upright stems above aromatic gray-green foliage, making it a striking contrast plant among purple-flowered lavenders. As a sterile hybrid it will not come true from seed and must be propagated from cuttings. Grow in full sun in lean, sharply drained soil, since wet roots in winter are far more damaging than cold air temperatures. Shear lightly after the main summer flush to maintain a tidy mound and encourage a second, lighter bloom.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun; its more compact habit suits tighter spacing than many lavandin selections.

directions: A more compact lavandin bred for smaller garden spaces, 'Gros Bleu' carries slender, tapering flower spikes with notably dark indigo calyxes beneath lavender-blue petals, giving the inflorescence a two-toned look. Its scent leans sweeter and less camphoraceous than many lavandin selections, making it a favorite for fresh bouquets as well as border planting. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, and expect a strong midsummer flush with the possibility of a lighter repeat bloom in a mild autumn. Prune back by about a third after flowering to keep plants compact and prevent the bare, woody centers common to older lavandins.

planting.note: Install rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with sharp drainage, giving ample room for a vigorous, spreading mound.

directions: An Australian-origin lavandin selection prized by growers for its vigor and generous aromatic oil output, 'Riverina Thomas' forms a large, mounded shrub of gray-green foliage topped with long, tapered purple-blue flower spikes in summer, with a chance of a lighter second flush in fall. Like other lavandins it is a sterile triploid hybrid and must be propagated by cuttings rather than seed. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, and avoid heavy, wet winter ground, which is the most common cause of lavandin decline. Cut plants back hard in early spring every few years to delay the woody, open centers that develop with age.

planting.note: Set out cutting-grown plants in spring in full sun, where the variegated foliage will color best and show off against the blue-violet flowers.

directions: Found as a variegated sport in a block of lavandin stock at an English nursery, 'Walberton's Silver Edge' is grown chiefly for its silvery-gray foliage crisply margined in cream, a trait that holds its color through the growing season independent of bloom time. Blue-violet flower spikes appear through summer on stems held above the patterned leaves, giving the plant ornamental interest even before flowering. Grow in full sun in lean, sharply drained soil; too much shade or overly rich soil can cause the variegation to fade and the habit to loosen. Shear lightly after bloom to maintain a dense, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in full sun with excellent drainage, allowing room for a broad, free-flowering mound.

directions: 'Dutch Mill' bears long, loosely branched flower stems topped with vivid grape-purple blooms that stand out against its silvery gray foliage, giving a showier flower color than many darker lavandins. It is counted among the hardier lavandin selections and performs well as a cut flower thanks to its long stems and large, open flower heads. Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil, since lavandins resent heavy or waterlogged ground far more than they mind cold. Shear the plant into a rounded form right after flowering to keep it compact and encourage dense new growth for the following season.
